summary.text: After complementing the cell states, a parity invariant rules out adjacent 1s and reduces the Rule 167 update to addition of the two diagonal neighbors modulo 2, so the complemented center is described by Pascal’s triangle: it vanishes at odd times and at time \(2m\) equals \(\binom{2m-1}{m-1}\bmod 2\). The binary-digit decomposition of binomial coefficients modulo 2 shows this coefficient is odd exactly when \(2m\) is a power of two, while \(n\mid 2^{n+1}\) holds exactly when \(n\) is a power of two; hence the new center bit is the complement of the floor-term indicator, and appending that bit to the binary prefix gives the claimed recurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let \(C(t,x)\in\{0,1\}\) denote the state at time \(t\in\mathbb N\) and position \(x\in\mathbb Z\) of the Rule 167 cellular automaton. Initially
\[
C(0,x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&x\ne0.\end{cases}
\]
If the three cells to the left, at the center, and to the right have values \(L,C,R\), the next value is the bit of 167 with index \(4L+2C+R\). Since
\[
167=(10100111)_2,
\]
the complete rule table, with triples ordered as \((L,C,R)\), is
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
(L,C,R)&000&001&010&011&100&101&110&111\\ \hline
\text{new state}&1&1&1&0&0&1&0&1.
\end{array}
\]
In particular every state remains either 0 or 1.

Write
\[
b_t=C(t,0)
\]
for the middle-column bit. The sequence in the statement is the integer represented by the prefix \(b_0b_1\cdots b_n\), namely
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n b_k2^{n-k}.
\]
We shall determine exactly when \(b_n=0\).

Define the complementary configuration
\[
v(t,x)=1-C(t,x).
\]
Thus \(v(t,x)=1\) exactly when \(C(t,x)=0\). Directly applying the Rule 167 table to the single-cell initial configuration gives
\[
C(1,x)=\begin{cases}0,&x=1,\\1,&x\ne1,\end{cases}
\qquad	ext{and hence}\qquad
v(1,x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=1,\\0,&x\ne1.
\end{cases}
\]
Indeed, at \(x=1\) the time-zero neighborhood is \(100\), whose output is 0; at \(x=0\) and \(x=-1\) the neighborhoods are respectively \(010\) and \(001\), and elsewhere the neighborhood is \(000\), all of whose outputs are 1.

Complementing every entry in the Rule 167 table gives the following transition table for \(v\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
(v_L,v_C,v_R)&000&001&010&011&100&101&110&111\\ \hline
\text{new }v&0&1&0&1&1&0&0&0.
\end{array}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
Here \(v_L=v(t,x-1)\), \(v_C=v(t,x)\), and \(v_R=v(t,x+1)\).

We next establish a parity restriction on the support of \(v\): for every \(t\ge1\),
\[
v(t,x)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\equiv t\pmod 2.             \tag{2}
\]
At \(t=1\), the only 1 occurs at \(x=1\), so this is true. Suppose it is true at time \(t\). Inspection of (1) shows that if \(v(t+1,x)=1\), then either \(v(t,x-1)=1\) or \(v(t,x+1)=1\): the triples producing 1 are \(001,011,100\). In the first case the induction hypothesis gives \(x-1\equiv t\pmod2\), hence \(x\equiv t+1\pmod2\). In the second case it gives \(x+1\equiv t\pmod2\), with the same conclusion. This proves (2) by induction.

It follows at once that two adjacent entries of \(v(t,\cdot)\) cannot both be 1 when \(t\ge1\), since adjacent integers have opposite parity. Consequently the patterns \(011,110,111\) in (1) can never occur at a positive time. On all the remaining possible patterns, (1) says precisely that the new value is the sum modulo 2 of the left and right values. Therefore, for every \(t\ge1\),
\[
v(t+1,x)\equiv v(t,x-1)+v(t,x+1)\pmod2,                         \tag{3}
\]
and both sides are understood as elements of \(\{0,1\}\).

Thus, beginning at time 1, the complementary automaton evolves by the mod-2 Pascal rule from a single 1 at position 1. We now write its explicit solution. For \(k\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z\), put
\[
F_k(x)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle {k\choose (x-1+k)/2}\pmod2,
 &x-1+k\text{ is even and }x-1+k\ge0,\\[6pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}                                                     \tag{4}
\]
As usual, \({k\choose r}=0\) if \(r>k\); thus (4) also automatically vanishes beyond the other edge of the light cone.

For \(k=0\), formula (4) is 1 exactly at \(x=1\), so \(F_0(x)=v(1,x)\). Moreover,
\[
F_{k+1}(x)\equiv F_k(x-1)+F_k(x+1)\pmod2.                        \tag{5}
\]
To see this, if \(x+k\) is odd, all three terms are zero by their parity conditions. If \(x+k\) is even and nonnegative, set \(r=(x+k)/2\). The term at \((k+1,x)\) is \({k+1\choose r}\), while the terms at \((k,x-1)\) and \((k,x+1)\) are respectively \({k\choose r-1}\) and \({k\choose r}\). Equation (5) is then Pascal’s identity
\[
{k+1\choose r}={k\choose r-1}+{k\choose r}
\]
reduced modulo 2. At the lower boundary \(x+k=0\), the first summand is zero and the other two are \({k\choose0}={k+1\choose0}=1\); if \(x+k<0\), all terms vanish. These observations also cover all boundary cases.

Equations (3), (5), and the common initial state imply by induction that
\[
v(k+1,x)=F_k(x)                                                   \tag{6}
\]
for every \(k\ge0\) and every integer \(x\).

We specialize (6) to the center \(x=0\). If the time is odd, say \(2m+1\), then \(k=2m\), and \(x-1+k=2m-1\) is odd. Hence
\[
v(2m+1,0)=F_{2m}(0)=0,
\qquad C(2m+1,0)=1.                                               \tag{7}
\]
If the time is even, say \(2m\) with \(m\ge1\), then \(k=2m-1\), and
\[
\frac{x-1+k}{2}=\frac{2m-2}{2}=m-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
v(2m,0)={2m-1\choose m-1}\pmod2
\]
and
\[
C(2m,0)=1-\left({2m-1\choose m-1}\bmod2\right).                 \tag{8}
\]

It remains to determine the parity of this binomial coefficient. We will use the following one-digit form of Lucas’s congruence modulo 2:
\[
{N\choose K}\equiv
{N\bmod2\choose K\bmod2}
{\lfloor N/2\rfloor\choose\lfloor K/2\rfloor}
\pmod2.                                                          \tag{9}
\]
For completeness, this follows by working over the field \(\mathbb F_2\). If \(N=2q+\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\in\{0,1\}\), then
\[
(1+X)^N=(1+X)^\epsilon((1+X)^2)^q
       =(1+X)^\epsilon(1+X^2)^q
\]
in \(\mathbb F_2[X]\). Comparing the coefficient of \(X^K\), and writing \(K=2r+\delta\), gives (9).

We first need the auxiliary fact
\[
{2j\choose j}\equiv0\pmod2\qquad(j\ge1).                        \tag{10}
\]
This can be proved by strong induction on \(j\). If \(j\) is odd, (9) has the factor
\({0\choose1}=0\), so the coefficient is even. If \(j\) is even, write \(j=2\ell\). Formula (9) gives
\[
{2j\choose j}={4\ell\choose2\ell}
 \equiv {0\choose0}{2\ell\choose\ell}
 \equiv {2\ell\choose\ell}\pmod2.
\]
Here \(1\le\ell<j\), so the last coefficient is even by induction. This proves (10).

We now prove, for every \(m\ge1\),
\[
{2m-1\choose m-1}\equiv1\pmod2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2m\text{ is a power of }2.                                      \tag{11}
\]
Use strong induction on \(m\). For \(m=1\), the coefficient is \({1\choose0}=1\), and \(2m=2=2^1\).

Suppose first that \(m\) is even, say \(m=2q\). Then \(m-1=2q-1\) is odd. Applying (9) gives
\[
{2m-1\choose m-1}
={4q-1\choose2q-1}
\equiv {1\choose1}{2q-1\choose q-1}
\equiv {2q-1\choose q-1}\pmod2.                                 \tag{12}
\]
Since \(q<m\), the induction hypothesis says that the last coefficient is odd exactly when \(2q\) is a power of 2. But \(2m=4q=2(2q)\) is a power of 2 exactly when \(2q\) is a power of 2. Thus (11) holds in the even case.

Suppose next that \(m>1\) is odd, say \(m=2j+1\). Then \(j\ge1\), and (9) gives
\[
{2m-1\choose m-1}
={4j+1\choose2j}
\equiv {1\choose0}{2j\choose j}
\equiv0\pmod2                                                     \tag{13}
\]
by (10). On the other hand
\[
2m=4j+2\equiv2\pmod4.
\]
Since \(m>1\), this number is at least 6. A power of 2 at least 4 is divisible by 4, so \(2m\) cannot be a power of 2. Both sides of (11) are therefore false in this case. This completes the induction and proves (11).

Combining (7), (8), and (11), we obtain, for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
C(n,0)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\text{ is a power of }2.                                       \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, if \(n\) is odd, (7) says that its center state is 1, and an odd \(n\ge2\) is not a power of 2. If \(n=2m\), equation (8) says that its center state is 0 exactly when the coefficient in (11) is odd, which is exactly when \(n=2m\) is a power of 2.

We next relate (14) to the floor term in the conjecture. For \(n\ge2\), let
\[
r=2^{n+1}\bmod n.
\]
Because \(r\) is a nonnegative integer,
\[
\left\lfloor(1/2)^r\right\rfloor
=
\begin{cases}1,&r=0,\\0,&r>0.
\end{cases}                                                     \tag{15}
\]
The condition \(r=0\) is equivalent to \(n\mid2^{n+1}\). We claim that
\[
n\mid2^{n+1}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\text{ is a power of }2.                                       \tag{16}
\]
If \(n\mid2^{n+1}\), every prime divisor of \(n\) must divide 2, so unique prime factorization gives \(n=2^s\) for some \(s\ge0\). Conversely, if \(n=2^s\), then \(s<2^s=n\), and hence \(s\le n+1\); therefore \(2^s\mid2^{n+1}\). This proves (16).

Let
\[
E(n)=\left\lfloor(1/2)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor.
\]
Equations (15) and (16) show that, for \(n\ge2\), \(E(n)=1\) exactly when \(n\) is a power of 2, and otherwise \(E(n)=0\). Comparing with (14), and remembering that both \(C(n,0)\) and \(E(n)\) belong to \(\{0,1\}\), gives
\[
b_n=C(n,0)=1-E(n)                                               \tag{17}
\]
for every \(n\ge2\).

Finally, the definition of the binary-prefix integer immediately yields its elementary recurrence. For every \(n\ge1\), separate the final term in the defining sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k2^{n-k}+b_n\\
&=2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k2^{n-1-k}+b_n\\
&=2a(n-1)+b_n.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{18}
\]
For \(n\ge2\), substitute (17) into (18). We conclude that
\[
\boxed{
 a(n)=2a(n-1)+1-
 \left\lfloor(1/2)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor
}
\]
for every integer \(n\ge2\), as required.
